The Supreme Court’s unsigned order on June 2, 2026, stayed a lower court injunction and allowed Alabama to use its 2023 legislatively enacted congressional map for the 2026 elections. This is not “plainly wrong,” not “a final nail in the coffin of the Voting Rights Act,” and not evidence that the Court is “back-pedaling its own precedent” to serve “the whims of this president.” Background (facts, not spin) After the 2020 census, Alabama’s Republican legislature drew a map with one majority-Black or Black-opportunity district out of seven. Black residents make up roughly 27% of Alabama’s population. A strictly proportional outcome would suggest about 1.9 seats. In Allen v. Milligan (2023), a 5-4 Supreme Court (Roberts joining the three liberals) held that the prior map likely violated Section 2 of the VRA under the Gingles framework and required Alabama to draw a second district in which Black voters had a realistic opportunity to elect their preferred candidate. Alabama then enacted the 2023 map (still only one such district). A three-judge district court later found it was the product of intentional racial discrimination and ordered a different map drawn by a special master. In April 2026, the Supreme Court decided Louisiana v. Callais, which clarified and tightened the standards for Section 2 claims — making it harder for plaintiffs to prevail by requiring stricter adherence to traditional districting criteria and raising the bar on racial predominance claims. The district court’s analysis in the Alabama case departed from that new precedent. SCOTUS therefore stayed the injunction in a 6-3 order (conservative majority; the three liberals dissented). The practical result: Alabama will use its 2023 map (6 Republican-leaning districts, 1 Democratic-leaning) rather than a court-imposed alternative for the 2026 midterms. Addressing the specific claims “Coordinated attempt to rewrite the rules in favor of Congressional Republicans”Redistricting is a core legislative function assigned to state legislatures by the Constitution. When Republicans control the Alabama legislature, they draw maps that maximize Republican seats — just as Democrats do in states they control (Illinois, New York, etc.). This is aggressive partisan gerrymandering. It is not new, and it is not uniquely a Republican sin. Federal courts largely stay out of partisan gerrymandering claims after Rucho v. Common Cause (2019). The VRA Section 2 inquiry is supposed to be about racial vote dilution, not partisan outcomes. “Puts in use the very map that this same court had previously deemed racially discriminatory”This is misleading. Milligan addressed an earlier map. The 2023 map was Alabama’s response. The lower court’s finding of intentional discrimination in the 2023 map was not a final Supreme Court ruling — it was a district court decision that SCOTUS has now stayed because it conflicted with intervening precedent (Callais). Staying an injunction pending further review is standard appellate practice, especially close to an election (the Purcell principle cautions against last-minute changes that disrupt election administration). “Final nail in the coffin of the Voting Rights Act” / “diminishing the power of Black voices” / “disenfranchise”This rhetoric is overheated and inaccurate. No Black voter in Alabama is being prevented from registering, casting a ballot, or having that ballot counted. “Disenfranchise” has a specific meaning; it does not mean “the map makes it harder for my preferred party to win a second seat.” Section 2 prohibits dilution of minority voting strength. It does not guarantee proportional representation or require states to draw the maximum possible number of minority-opportunity districts regardless of traditional criteria (compactness, contiguity, respect for political subdivisions, communities of interest). SCOTUS has long held that race cannot be the predominant factor in drawing districts (Shaw v. Reno, Miller v. Johnson). Post-Callais, the bar is higher. The Court is refining — not abolishing — Section 2 jurisprudence. The VRA remains in force; its interpretation has evolved, as it has for decades. “SCOTUS has once again proved it is willing to back-peddle its own precedent in favor of the whims of this president.”This is the weakest and most partisan part of the post. The order is unsigned and cites the district court’s departure from Louisiana v. Callais (decided April 2026). That is legal reasoning, not presidential dictation. Presidents do not “whim” Supreme Court stays. The Trump administration supported Alabama’s position (as prior administrations have supported states in redistricting fights), but the justices decide based on the record and precedent. If the Court were simply rubber-stamping the executive, we would not have seen the 2023 Milligan decision itself, which went against the Alabama Republican map at the time. Bottom line Alabama’s 2023 map produces a 6–1 Republican advantage in a state that reliably votes Republican at the presidential and statewide level. That outcome is politically advantageous to one party. Whether it also violates Section 2 of the VRA after Callais is a contested legal question. The Supreme Court has temporarily resolved the emergency application in favor of letting the legislatively enacted map stand for the upcoming election rather than imposing a court-drawn alternative. That is a procedural and legal judgment about precedent, timing, and institutional roles — not a conspiracy to “disenfranchise Black voices.” Strong rhetoric about “nails in coffins” and presidential “whims” may rally a base, but it does not accurately describe what the Court did or why. Redistricting fights are hardball politics dressed up in civil-rights language on both sides. The durable solution remains what it has always been: win state legislative majorities and draw the maps yourself, or persuade courts under the actual current legal standard. This decision keeps Alabama’s elected representatives’ map in place for 2026 while the underlying litigation continues on a fuller record. That is neither the end of the Voting Rights Act nor a subversion of democracy. It is the Supreme Court doing what appellate courts do: correcting lower-court departures from its own recent precedent on an expedited basis.
